newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian republic seen boosting Asian standing.
newsitem.headline: Australian republic seen boosting Asian standing.

text.p: An Australian republic would establish the country's independence in the eyes of Asia and be freer to define its future, say supporters of a move to sever more than 200 years of constitutional ties with Britain.

Although Australia has in effect been independent of Britain for many years, becoming a republic is seen as having a symbolic power affecting all Australians, particularly the ever growing number from non-English speaking backgrounds.

"The important thing is that Australia will have a constitution that says it is a sovereign independent nation," said historian Donald Horne, an active campaigner for an Australian republic for 30 years.
"Around that can be built a more realistic view about what it means to be an Australian," Horne told Reuters on Tuesday.

Prime Minister John Howard said on Tuesday the government would hold a convention this year to consider how to become a republic, replacing Britain's Queen Elizabeth with an Australian head-of-state. A nationwide vote could be held by 1999.

Horne, who coined the phrase "The Lucky Country" in the 1960s, said Australia currently has a "black hole" at the centre of its symbolic structure as many Australians do not believe the Queen should be head-of-state.
A change to a republic would also help clear misconceptions and confusion about Australia in Asia, said John Menadue, an advisor to the Research Institute for Asia & the Pacific.
A former Australian ambassador to Japan in the late 1970s, Menadue recalled having the New Zealand flag hoisted when he offered his credentials to the Japanese emperor.
And a senior Japanese businessman offered an honorary Order of Australia told Menadue he wanted to visit Buckingham Palace to have the award presented.
Such misconceptions showed Australia was not clearly defined in Asian minds, even at the highest levels, Menadue said.
There was also confusion in Asia about whether Australia was really a part of the Asia-Pacific region, a belief it tried hard to promote under former Labor prime minister Paul Keating.
For Australians from non-English speaking backgrounds, a move to a republic would instil a sense of belonging to an independent nation, said Henry Tsang, Chinese-born deputy Lord Mayor of Sydney.
"This is very important for a community that wants to start a new life with a new lifestyle and a new future," Tsang said.

"They want to make the commitment to a nation which has its own destiny," he said. Tsang said it was difficult for Chinese Australians to convince friends and relatives overseas that Australia was not just a colony of Britain.
"Newer Australians are very proud of the potential there is (here), and can see what we can achieve," Tsang said. "Culture is ever changing, no culture stays stagnant."

A republican Australia, however, will still value trade links with Britain. The relationship between the two countries has been eroded as Britain has increasingly been drawn into Europe, but trade remains strong.

Britain is the second largest foreign investor in Australia, behind the United States, investing A$27.7 billion (US$21 billion) in 1995. Australia is the third largest foreign investor in the U.K., according to the British Consulate.
Roger Pratt, chairman of the Australian British Chamber of Commerce, said this was unlikely to change under a republic.
"Trade relations between Britain and Australia are based on hard-headed bottom line decisions, not political issues."

But for republicans the issue of the head-of-state remains paramount. Becoming a republic means Australia's national symbols would be unambiguously and unequivocally Australian, said lawyer Malcolm Turnbull, chairman of the Australian Republican Movement.
"Unless you think that the office of head-of-state is an irrelevance and is of no importance, then plainly that head-of-state should be an Australian citizen," said Turnbull.
"It's summed up very nicely in a very simple phrase: We should have a resident for president," he ssaid.
